fields.title: The Second Letter to Timothy
fields.subtitle: Pros Timotheon B, “Second to Timothy”
fields.description: Paul’s last letter, written in chains in Rome to Timothy, the younger man he called his dear son, as he waited for the verdict he expected to be death. Do not be ashamed; stir up the gift God gave you, for God has not given us a spirit of fear; be strong, like a soldier, an athlete and a farmer; handle the message of truth correctly and correct opponents gently; continue in the Scriptures, all of them breathed out by God; preach the word. Then Paul’s farewell — “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” — and his requests: come before winter, bring Mark, bring my cloak and my scrolls. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Second Letter to Timothy?
qa.answer: A letter in the New Testament from the apostle Paul, imprisoned in Rome, to his co-worker Timothy, probably in Ephesus. It is the most personal of the three Pastoral Letters. Paul urges Timothy not to be ashamed of the gospel or of him, to guard what has been entrusted to him and pass it on, to endure suffering, to hold to the Scriptures and to preach the word. It ends with Paul’s farewell and with requests and news about friends who have deserted him or stood by him.

qa.question: Who wrote 2 Timothy, and when?
qa.answer: The letter names Paul as its author, and the church has read it as his last letter, written during a second imprisonment in Rome shortly before his execution under Nero, in the mid 60s AD; the historian Eusebius records this tradition. Many modern scholars think the Pastoral Letters were written after Paul’s death by a follower, though some of them think this letter preserves genuine notes from Paul. Others hold that its many personal details are best explained as Paul’s own.

qa.question: What does 2 Timothy 3:16 mean when it says Scripture is “breathed out by God”?
qa.answer: The Greek word, used only here in the Bible, is literally “God-breathed”. Paul says that all Scripture comes from God, as breath comes from a mouth, and is therefore “useful for teaching, for rebuking, for correcting and for training in righteousness” (3:16), so that God’s people are equipped for every good work. He was speaking of the Jewish Scriptures, the Old Testament, which Timothy had known from infancy; Christians have applied the same words to the New Testament as well.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
That is why I am suffering as I am. But I am not ashamed, because I know the one I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard what I have entrusted to him until that day.

— 2 Timothy 1:12

This is a letter from a prison cell, written by a man who expects to die. Paul is in chains in Rome. Most of his friends have gone. He has already faced one hearing with no one to stand beside him, and he knows how the next one is likely to end. Winter is coming, and he wants his cloak. Above all, he wants to see Timothy once more.

If, as the church has long believed, it is the last letter Paul wrote, then these are the final words we have from the apostle who carried the gospel across the Roman world. They are not the words of a defeated man. They are full of thanksgiving, courage and charge, and of the plain confidence that the one he has trusted will keep what he has entrusted to him.

A letter from prison

Paul had been a prisoner in Rome before, under house arrest, free to receive visitors and to preach, as Acts ends (Acts 28:30–31). This imprisonment is harsher. He is “chained like a criminal”. When Onesiphorus came to Rome, he had to search hard to find him. The church historian Eusebius, writing in the fourth century, records that Paul was released after his first imprisonment, preached again, and was arrested a second time, and that in this imprisonment he wrote his second letter to Timothy. Tradition holds that he was beheaded in Rome under Nero, in the mid 60s.

As with the other Pastoral Letters, many modern scholars think this one was written after Paul’s death by a follower who honoured his memory; some who hold that view think it preserves genuine notes from Paul’s last days. Others find its personal detail, the names, the cloak, the parchments, the grief, very hard to explain as anything but Paul’s own. The introduction to 1 Timothy in this edition says more about the question.

Timothy seems to have been in Ephesus, or nearby in the province of Asia. Paul asks him to come before winter, when ships stopped sailing, and to bring Mark with him.

The shape of the letter

  • Chapter 1: do not be ashamed. Thanks for Timothy’s faith, a call to stir up his gift and share in suffering, and news of who has deserted Paul and who has stood by him.
  • Chapter 2: be strong. The soldier, the athlete and the farmer; a trustworthy saying; how to handle the truth and how to treat those who oppose it.
  • Chapter 3: continue in what you have learned. Terrible times, Paul’s own example, and the Scriptures that make a person wise for salvation.
  • Chapter 4: preach the word. A last charge, Paul’s farewell, and personal requests and greetings.

Stir up the gift

Paul begins with memories. He remembers Timothy’s tears at their last parting, and the faith that “first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice”. The gospel came to Timothy through a family, and Paul wants him to know it is truly his.

Then the first great charge:

That is why I remind you to stir up into flame the gift God gave you when I laid my hands on you. For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but a spirit of power and love and sound judgment.

— 2 Timothy 1:6–7

Timothy may have been tempted to keep his head down. To be linked with a prisoner, and a prisoner of Rome, was dangerous and shameful. Paul tells him not to be ashamed of the Lord or of him, but to share in suffering for the gospel, “relying on the power of God”. The God who calls us to suffer is the one who saved us, “not because of anything we had done but because of his own purpose and grace”, and who through Christ “has destroyed death and has brought life and immortality to light.”

The chapter ends with two lists of names. “Everyone in the province of Asia has deserted me,” Paul writes. But Onesiphorus “often refreshed me and was not ashamed that I was in chains.” It is a small, human moment, and a reminder that faithfulness is often a matter of simply turning up.

Soldier, athlete, farmer

Chapter 2 opens with a chain of four generations: what Timothy heard from Paul, he is to pass on to trustworthy people, who will teach others as well. That is how the gospel has always travelled. Then Paul gives three pictures of the life it calls for: the soldier who does not get tangled in civilian affairs, the athlete who competes by the rules, the hardworking farmer who eats first from the harvest. Each speaks of single-mindedness, discipline and patience.

“Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead and descended from David,” Paul writes. He is in chains for this gospel. “But God’s word is not chained.” And he quotes what seems to be a saying the churches already knew:

Here is a saying you can rely on: If we died with him, we will also live with him. If we endure, we will also reign with him. If we deny him, he will also deny us. If we are unfaithful, he remains faithful, for he cannot be false to himself.

— 2 Timothy 2:11–13

The last line breaks the pattern. Each line so far has matched what we do with what he does. But if we are unfaithful, he does not become unfaithful in return. Most readers hear in it the deepest assurance of the letter; some hear also a warning that he stays true to every word, including the one before it. Either way, his faithfulness does not hang on ours.

A worker with nothing to be ashamed of

Timothy is to avoid quarrels about words and “godless, empty chatter”. Two teachers, Hymenaeus and Philetus, were saying that the resurrection had already taken place, perhaps meaning that it was only spiritual, and they were destroying the faith of some. Against all this, Paul gives Timothy a single aim: “Make every effort to stand before God tested and approved, a worker with nothing to be ashamed of, who handles the message of truth correctly.”

Then he describes how such a worker treats opponents. “The Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach and patient with difficult people, gently correcting those who oppose him.” The goal is not to win but to see them come to their senses and escape the devil’s trap. It is one of the most searching passages in the New Testament for anyone who has to defend the truth.

All Scripture

Paul warns that “in the last days there will be terrible times”, and describes people who “love themselves and love money”, who keep up an appearance of godliness but deny its power. Some read the last days as the whole time between Christ’s first coming and his return; others as a time still ahead. Paul plainly expects Timothy to meet such people now.

Against them he sets two things: Paul’s own example, his teaching, way of life and sufferings, which Timothy has seen; and the Scriptures Timothy has known since infancy, “which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.” Then comes the verse that has shaped the church’s understanding of the Bible more than any other:

All Scripture is breathed out by God and is useful for teaching, for rebuking, for correcting and for training in righteousness, so that the one who belongs to God may be fully capable, equipped for every good work.

— 2 Timothy 3:16–17

Paul was speaking of the Jewish Scriptures, what Christians call the Old Testament. The church has applied his words to the New Testament too, since it came to be recognized as Scripture alongside them.

Preach the word

The last chapter opens with Paul’s most solemn charge, made “in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead”: “Preach the word. Be ready whether the time seems right or not.” A time is coming when people will want teachers who tell them what their ears itch for. Timothy must keep a clear head, endure hardship and “do the work of an evangelist”.

Then Paul speaks of himself:

For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time for my departure has come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.

— 2 Timothy 4:6–7

A drink offering was wine poured out on the altar to complete a sacrifice. Paul sees his coming death as the last part of an offering his whole life has been.

The cloak and the scrolls

And then, astonishingly, the letter turns practical. Demas, “in love with this present world”, has deserted. “Only Luke is with me.” Bring Mark, “because he is helpful to me in my work”: the young man Paul once refused to take with him (Acts 15:37–39) has become a friend he wants at the end. Bring the cloak I left at Troas, “and my scrolls, especially the parchments.” Beware of Alexander the metalworker. “Do your best to get here before winter.”

Readers have been moved by these lines for centuries. In 1535, imprisoned in the castle of Vilvoorde near Brussels, William Tyndale wrote asking for a warmer cap, a warmer coat, and above all his Hebrew Bible, grammar and dictionary, so that he could go on translating. He was executed the following year. Like Paul, he wanted the Scriptures to the end.

How to read 2 Timothy

Read it in one sitting, as a last letter. Hear the loneliness in it and the courage. Notice how often Paul speaks of shame and of not being ashamed, of suffering and of guarding what has been entrusted. Notice how many people are named, for good and ill. And read it alongside 1 Timothy, to see the same friendship at two different moments.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in 2 Timothy are worth knowing about before you begin.

“Breathed out by God” (3:16). The Greek word is literally “God-breathed”. Where older Bibles say “given by inspiration of God”, this translation keeps the picture of Scripture coming from God’s breath, as his word goes out of his mouth.

“What I have entrusted to him” (1:12). The Greek says “my deposit”. It may mean what Paul has entrusted to God, his life and work, or the gospel God has entrusted to Paul, as in 1:14. Because God is the one who guards it here, the translation follows the first reading.

“Sound judgment” (1:7). The word in older Bibles is “a sound mind”. It means clear thinking and self-control, the opposite of panic.

“The one who belongs to God” (3:17). The Greek has “the man of God”, a title of prophets and leaders. Here it probably includes any believer, and the translation says so.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: 2 Timothy 1
fields.body_html:
Greeting

From Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, sent to proclaim the promise of life that is in Christ Jesus, to Timothy, my dear son. Grace, mercy and peace to you from God the Father and from Christ Jesus our Lord.

Thanks for Timothy’s sincere faith

I thank God, whom I serve with a clear conscience as my ancestors did, whenever I remember you in my prayers, as I do night and day. I remember your tears, and I long to see you, so that my joy may be complete. I recall your sincere faith, which first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice, and which I am sure now lives in you. That is why I remind you to stir up into flame the gift God gave you when I laid my hands on you. For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but a spirit of power and love and sound judgment.

Not ashamed of the gospel

So do not be ashamed to testify about our Lord, or ashamed of me, his prisoner. Instead, share with me in suffering for the gospel, relying on the power of God. He saved us and called us to a holy life, not because of anything we had done but because of his own purpose and grace. This grace was given us in Christ Jesus before eternal ages began, and now it has been revealed through the appearing of our Savior, Jesus Christ. He has destroyed death and has brought life and immortality to light through the gospel. For this gospel I was appointed a herald, an apostle and a teacher. That is why I am suffering as I am. But I am not ashamed, because I know the one I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard what I have entrusted to him until that day. Keep to the pattern of sound teaching you heard from me, with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. Guard the good treasure entrusted to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit who lives in us.

Deserted by many, refreshed by Onesiphorus

You know that everyone in the province of Asia has deserted me, including Phygelus and Hermogenes. May the Lord show mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed that I was in chains. Instead, when he came to Rome, he searched hard for me until he found me. May the Lord grant that he find mercy from the Lord on that day. And you know very well all the ways he helped in Ephesus.

fields.title: 2 Timothy 2
fields.body_html:
A good soldier of Christ Jesus

So you, my son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. And what you heard from me before many witnesses, pass on to trustworthy people who will be able to teach others as well. Join with me in suffering, like a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier on active duty gets tangled up in civilian affairs; he wants to please the officer who enlisted him. In the same way, an athlete does not receive the winner’s crown unless he competes by the rules. The farmer who does the hard work should be the first to eat from the harvest. Reflect on what I am saying, for the Lord will give you understanding in all things.

God’s word is not chained

Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead and descended from David, as my gospel proclaims. For this gospel I am suffering, even to the point of being chained like a criminal. But God’s word is not chained. So I endure everything for the sake of God’s chosen people, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, and with it eternal glory. Here is a saying you can rely on: If we died with him, we will also live with him. If we endure, we will also reign with him. If we deny him, he will also deny us. If we are unfaithful, he remains faithful, for he cannot be false to himself.

A worker approved by God

Keep reminding people of these things, and warn them before the Lord not to quarrel about words. It does no good and only ruins those who listen. Make every effort to stand before God tested and approved, a worker with nothing to be ashamed of, who handles the message of truth correctly. Stay away from godless, empty chatter, because those who indulge in it will become more and more ungodly, and their teaching will spread like gangrene. Hymenaeus and Philetus are among them. They have wandered away from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they are destroying the faith of some. But God’s solid foundation stands firm, sealed with these words: “The Lord knows those who are his,” and “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord must turn away from wickedness.”

Vessels for special use

In a large house there are not only gold and silver dishes but also wooden and clay ones, some for special occasions and some for common use. Those who keep themselves clean from such things will be vessels for special use, made holy, useful to the master, and ready for every good work. Run away from the passions of youth, and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace, together with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart. Have nothing to do with foolish and ignorant arguments; you know they only lead to quarrels. The Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach and patient with difficult people, gently correcting those who oppose him. Perhaps God will grant them repentance and they will come to know the truth, and come to their senses and escape the trap of the devil, who has held them captive to do his will.

fields.title: 2 Timothy 3
fields.body_html:
Terrible times in the last days

But understand this: in the last days there will be terrible times. People will love themselves and love money. They will be boastful, arrogant and abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful and unholy. They will be without love, unforgiving, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, hating what is good. They will be treacherous, reckless and conceited, loving pleasure rather than loving God. They will keep up an appearance of godliness, but deny its power. Have nothing to do with such people. Among them are those who worm their way into homes and gain control over vulnerable women who are weighed down with sins and swayed by all kinds of desires, always learning but never able to come to a knowledge of the truth. Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these people oppose the truth. Their minds are corrupt, and they have failed the test of faith. But they will not get very far, because, as with those two, their folly will be clear to everyone.

Continue in what you have learned

But you know all about my teaching, my way of life, my purpose, my faith, my patience, my love, my endurance, my persecutions and sufferings, the things that happened to me in Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, and the persecutions I endured. Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them. In fact, everyone who wants to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted. But evil people and impostors will go from bad to worse, deceiving others and being deceived themselves. But as for you, continue in what you have learned and are sure of, since you know who taught you, and how from infancy you have known the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. All Scripture is breathed out by God and is useful for teaching, for rebuking, for correcting and for training in righteousness, so that the one who belongs to God may be fully capable, equipped for every good work.

fields.title: 2 Timothy 4
fields.body_html:
Preach the word

I solemnly charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and in view of his appearing and his kingdom: Preach the word. Be ready whether the time seems right or not. Correct, rebuke and encourage, with great patience and careful teaching. For a time will come when people will not put up with sound teaching. Instead, wanting to hear what their ears itch for, they will gather around them a great number of teachers to suit their own desires. They will turn away from listening to the truth and wander off into myths. But you, keep a clear head in every situation. Endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist, and carry out your ministry fully.

I have finished the race

For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time for my departure has come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Now there is waiting for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have longed for his appearing.

Come to me soon

Do your best to come to me soon. Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia and Titus to Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is helpful to me in my work. I have sent Tychicus to Ephesus. When you come, bring the cloak I left with Carpus at Troas, and my scrolls, especially the parchments. Alexander the metalworker did me a great deal of harm. The Lord will repay him for what he has done. You too should be on guard against him, because he strongly opposed our message.

The Lord stood by me

At my first defense no one came to support me; everyone deserted me. May it not be held against them. But the Lord stood by me and gave me strength, so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed and all the Gentiles might hear it. And I was rescued from the lion’s mouth. The Lord will rescue me from every evil attack and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. To him be the glory for ever and ever. Amen.

Final greetings

Greet Prisca and Aquila and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus stayed in Corinth, and I left Trophimus sick in Miletus.

Do your best to get here before winter.

Eubulus sends you greetings, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia and all the brothers and sisters.

The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you all.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Now there is waiting for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have longed for his appearing.

— 2 Timothy 4:8

Paul’s last look is forward. Behind him are the race, the fight and the faith he kept; around him are chains, cold and empty seats where his friends should be. But ahead of him is a crown, given by a righteous judge, on “that day”. And he will not wear it alone. It is for “all who have longed for his appearing”, which means it is for Timothy too, and for every reader who loves the Lord’s coming.

The question the letter leaves

Who will carry it on? That is the anxious question under the whole letter. Paul is about to die. The churches of Asia have turned away from him. False teachers are spreading. Demas has gone. Everything seems to depend on one young, gifted, perhaps fearful man. So Paul tells him to stir up the gift, to guard the treasure, to pass it on to trustworthy people, to continue in the Scriptures and to preach the word.

But the letter is just as clear that it does not finally depend on Timothy, or on Paul. “God’s word is not chained.” “God’s solid foundation stands firm.” “He remains faithful.” “The Lord stood by me and gave me strength.” The one Paul has believed is able to guard what Paul has entrusted to him. The gospel has outlived Paul’s chains, and Nero’s empire, and every generation since, because the Lord who stood by Paul has stood by his people still.

Every reader is in Timothy’s place: given something precious by those who went before, and asked to hand it on. For most of us that will not mean a prison cell. It may mean a grandmother’s faith passed to a grandchild, a Bible class faithfully taught, a friend visited when others stay away, as Onesiphorus searched Rome until he found Paul.

Where to go from here

This library holds many who heard Paul’s charge as addressed to them:

  • On the gift and the fire (1:6–7). Gareth Evans’s sermon Guard the Fire, preached on Pentecost Sunday.
  • On the Scriptures (3:14–17). John Calvin’s sermon All Scripture Is Given by Inspiration, on 3:16–17.
  • On preaching the word (4:1–5). Charles H. Spurgeon’s Lectures to My Students and An All-Round Ministry, his addresses to ministers; and John Chrysostom’s On the Priesthood.
  • On Paul’s last imprisonment and death. Eusebius’s The Church History, whose second book quotes this letter in telling of Paul’s first defense and his martyrdom in Rome; and The First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, written from Rome a generation later, which remembers Paul as “a striking example of patience”.
  • On keeping the faith to the end (4:7). The Epistle and Martyrdom of Polycarp, the account of an old bishop who would not deny his King; and Fox’s Book of Martyrs, which begins with the apostles, Paul among them, and tells of William Tyndale’s imprisonment and death at Vilvoorde.

And read 1 Timothy and Titus, in this same edition, to see the same apostle earlier, setting churches in order.

Every reference to 2 Timothy in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather what the great writers of the church have said about each passage. But the best next step may be to read the letter again, slowly, as the last words of a friend, and to take its confidence for your own:

The Lord will rescue me from every evil attack and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. To him be the glory for ever and ever. Amen.

— 2 Timothy 4:18
